title: Defective viral genomes of porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus type 2: Generation, characterization and interference effects on viral replication.
abstract: Porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus type 2 (PRRSV-2) is a major swine pathogen that causes substantial economic losses worldwide. Defective viral genomes (DVGs) are important regulators of viral replication, persistence, and evolution in many RNA viruses. However, the characteristics and functions of DVGs generated during PRRSV-2 infection remain unknown. Here, we systematically analyzed publicly available high-throughput sequencing datasets and characterized DVGs generated during both in vitro and in vivo PRRSV-2 infection. We found that PRRSV-2 preferentially generates large deletion DVGs, particularly in porcine alveolar macrophages (PAMs), and that DVG formation is associated with microhomology sequences, RNA secondary structure and AU-rich sequences. Break positions were enriched in the GP5/M genomic region, whereas rejoin positions clustered predominantly within the nsp1/nsp2 genomic region of the PRRSV-2 genome. Notably, the deletion events within the same gene were highly enriched in the nsp2 region, where multiple naturally occurring nsp2 deletion sites overlapped with DVG junction sites. These findings suggest that DVG-associated recombination may contribute to the formation of PRRSV-2 nsp2 deletion variants. Functionally, PRRSV-2-derived DVGs exhibited potent broad-spectrum antiviral activity against multiple prevalent PRRSV-2 lineage strains and PRRSV-1. Overall, our findings provide the first systematic characterization of PRRSV-2 DVGs, reveal a potential evolutionary link between DVGs and nsp2 deletion variants, and highlight the antiviral potential of PRRSV-2 DVGs.

title: Adaptation of a Fluorogenic RNA to N1-Methylpseudouridine Nucleoside Chemistry.
abstract: N1-methylpseudouridine (mΨ) is a modified nucleoside that entirely replaces uridine in the design of many therapeutic messenger RNAs (mRNA) to alleviate their intrinsic immunogenicity while preserving their capacity to be translated into protein. However, the impact of such replacement in functional non-coding RNAs has only been scarcely studied, and most studies have shown impairment in the function of the tested RNAs thereby limiting their potential applications. In this work, we further show that exchanging uridines by mΨ in green-emitting Fluorogenic Light-up Aptamers (FLAP) is detrimental to their capacity of binding and enhancing the fluorescence of their cognate fluorogen. Moreover, combining directed evolution and rational design allowed not only to pinpoint the structural elements impacted by the replacement of uridine by mΨ, but also to re-establish the function of a mΨ-modified non-coding RNA for the first time. This yielded Ψ-Spinach, a FLAP suited for the precise labelling of mΨ-modified mRNA and usable for human cells transfection. This work thus paves the way for the adaptation of other functional non-coding RNAs with mΨ in view of engineering and optimizing therapeutic modified mRNAs.

title: A ubiquitin network safeguards cell identity by continuously degrading a stem cell-related translational machinery.
abstract: How cell identity is maintained is a fundamental question, and loss of cell identity is a hallmark of aging associated with multiple age-related diseases. In the adult Drosophila midgut, we identified a posttranscriptional regulatory layer that supervises enterocyte (EC) identity and fails upon aging. Combining single-cell RNA-seq with lineage tracing in aging ECs and classical genetics, we found that aging ECs express genes that unlock the differentiated state. Upon aging, the protein Rogue (CG13928), a translational repressor, along with its partner, Orb2, orchestrates reactivation of a stem cell-related translational repression machinery involving P-body-associated RNA-binding proteins canceling the differentiated state. In young ECs, this machinery is continuously suppressed by the deubiquitinase nonstop (dUSP22) and the ubiquitin E2 dUbcH8/Kdo and E3 CTLH complex, mediating the degradation of the stem cell-related RNA binding proteins safeguarding EC identity. Upon aging, levels of dUSP22 decline and Rogue is ectopically expressed. RNA immunoprecipitation followed by nanopore-based direct RNA sequencing identified that Rogue binds to the RNA transcripts of dUbcH8/Kdo and eEF2, shortening their poly(A) tail and suppressing Kdo protein, resulting in accelerated proteasomal clearance of the CTLH complex. Subsequently, the stem cell-related P-bodies are reactivated, leading to decline in EC gene signatures and unlocking EC identity.

title: Building computational benchmarks: an Omnibenchmark reimplementation of a single-cell preprocessing pipeline evaluation
abstract: Background: In the past few years, we have seen a veritable surge in single-cell (e.g., RNA-sequencing) techniques and datasets, enabling increasingly detailed characterization of cellular heterogeneity across tissues and conditions. This surge in single-cell techniques has been complemented by a large number of analysis frameworks and pipelines, and a large parameter space and researcher degrees of freedom to use them. Many neutral benchmarks have been presented for various computational tasks, but most make design decisions that render them incompatible with each other, e.g., through the use of different datasets, metrics, or parameter sets. Results: We showcase Omnibenchmark, a recently developed framework to build reproducible, extensible, and standardized method comparisons for an arms-length benchmark that evaluates five single-cell RNA sequencing pipelines, spanning filtering, normalization, dimensionality reduction, and clustering, on three datasets. The framework facilitates the broad investigation of pipelines used in single-cell data analysis while highlighting how the process of building benchmarks can be streamlined and unified. This standardization enables benchmarks to be extended in several directions, including broader parameter sweeps, comparisons across software versions and architectures, isolation of pipeline steps, and integration of additional pipelines, datasets, and metrics. As an example, our harmonization of pipelines highlighted that tools implement the (clustering) resolution parameter differently. Conclusions: Omnibenchmark provides a reproducible, extensible, and standardized approach for benchmarking. By unifying the process of benchmark construction, it can facilitate more consistent method comparisons and provides a foundation for broader, more flexible, and more sustainable benchmarking efforts.

title: The RNA-binding protein KHSRP drives prostate cancer progression through a DUSP6 dependent axis.
abstract: Prostate cancer (PCa) remains a major clinical challenge, particularly because of its progression to more aggressive disease states, and the molecular mechanisms driving its progression are still incompletely understood. KH-type splicing regulatory protein (KHSRP) is a multifunctional RNA-binding protein involved in post-transcriptional gene regulation, but its role and downstream regulatory mechanisms in PCa remain unclear. The clinical relevance of KHSRP in PCa was assessed using public datasets and patient specimens. We assessed the biological functions of KHSRP in vitro and in vivo, identified DUSP6 by integrative RNA-seq and RIP-seq analyses, and further validated the associated signaling and phenotypic changes using Western blotting and functional assays. KHSRP was significantly upregulated in PCa and was associated with aggressive clinicopathological features and poor prognosis. Functional experiments showed that KHSRP overexpression promoted proliferation, migration, and invasion while suppressing apoptosis in PCa cells, whereas KHSRP knockdown produced the opposite effects. Mechanistically, integrative RNA-seq and RIP-seq analyses identified DUSP6 as a candidate downstream target of KHSRP. Further validation using RNA immunoprecipitation assays and RNA decay assays demonstrated that KHSRP accelerated DUSP6 mRNA decay and repressed DUSP6 expression at the post-transcriptional level. Reduced DUSP6 expression was accompanied by enhanced ERK phosphorylation and coordinated activation of PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling. Restoration of DUSP6 attenuated the pro-tumorigenic effects of KHSRP and weakened the associated signaling activation. Xenograft assays further confirmed the tumor-promoting role of KHSRP in vivo. KHSRP drives PCa progression through a DUSP6-dependent signaling axis by repressing DUSP6 at the post-transcriptional level and facilitating coordinated activation of ERK and PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling. These findings identify a previously unrecognized KHSRP-DUSP6 regulatory axis in PCa and suggest that KHSRP may serve as a potential therapeutic target.

title: Structure of vesicular stomatitis virus L-P-N0 complex by cyro-electron microscopy.
abstract: The large protein (L) of nonsegmented, negative-strand RNA viruses, a viral order that includes rabies, Ebola, Nipah, and respiratory syncytial viruses, catalyze RNA-dependent RNA polymerization on nucleocapsid-sheathed RNA templates. L coordinates two distinct processes: messenger RNA (mRNA) transcription and genome replication. During transcription, L catalyzes cotranscriptional mRNA capping, methylation, and polyadenylation. The additional activities are not required during genome replication; instead, RNA synthesis is coupled to encapsidation by soluble nucleoprotein (N0) recruited by the phosphoprotein (P). We determined the structure of a vesicular stomatitis virus polymerase complex comprising L-P and N0. P directly engages the carboxyl-terminal domain of L (LCTD) to anchor N0 in a continuum of conformations including a more stable configuration with N0 positioned at the RNA-product exit channel, poised for encapsidation. This study reveals a function for LCTD in encapsidation of nascent RNAs and provides the structure of a polymerase complex required for genomic RNA replication.

title: FOSL1-associated condensates modulate superenhancer-mediated selected IL-1 family gene activation in psoriasis.
abstract: Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin disease involving abnormal keratinocyte gene expression, yet the upstream epigenetic mechanisms driving these alterations remain unclear. Here we performed multiomics analyses (chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing, CUT&Tag, ATAC-seq, and RNA sequencing) on psoriatic lesions, perilesional skin, healthy skin, and M5-stimulated HaCaT cells. Functional validation was performed using CRISPR-mediated superenhancer (SE) editing, epigenetic modulation, circular chromosome conformation capture sequencing, assay for chromatin-bound condensates by exploratory sequencing, coimmunoprecipitation, and fluorescence recovery after photobleaching. We found widespread activation of enhancers and SEs in lesions, including an interleukin 1 (IL-1)-SE regulating IL1A, IL1B, and IL36G transcription. BET inhibition reduced SE activity, repressed IL-1 cytokines, and relieved psoriasis-like inflammation in vivo. Fos-like antigen 1 (FOSL1) was identified as a key transcription factor enriched in active SEs and associated with condensate formation, contributing to the maintenance of EP300 occupancy and histone H3 lysine 27 acetylation deposition. Macrophage-derived IL-1 up-regulated FOSL1 through mitogen-activated protein kinase/ERK signaling, forming a positive feedback loop that amplified inflammation. This study revealed an FOSL1-SE-centered regulatory network driving keratinocyte inflammatory responses, providing previously unknown therapeutic targets for psoriasis.

title: Research and application progress of siRNA nano-delivery systems in gliomas.
abstract: Gliomas are the most common and highly harmful primary central nervous system tumors. Small interfering RNA (siRNA) has been proposed as a promising therapeutic strategy for glioma by specifically silencing target gene expression. However, the instability of siRNA and its poor permeability across the blood-brain barrier (BBB) and blood-brain tumor barrier (BBTB) have significantly limited its clinical application. Therefore, appropriate delivery systems are urgently required to enhance the stability and targeting efficiency of siRNA. Nano-delivery systems, due to advantages such as protecting siRNA from being degraded by enzymes, increasing the rate of drug entry into the brain, and enabling targeted delivery, have become an effective means to solve the problem of siRNA treatment for glioma. This review outlines the design strategies, types, and application progress of siRNA nano-delivery systems for glioma treatment. It focuses on how biological macromolecule-based, polymer-based, lipid-based, inorganic, and biomimetic systems overcome in vivo delivery barriers through their material properties and functional modifications. The review also covers the mechanisms by which siRNA inhibits glioma, the strategies carriers use to cross the BBB, and combination therapy approaches. It then discusses the current challenges in this field and the prospects for clinical translation.

title: Inhibitory activity and mechanism of a scorpion-derived peptide BmKDfsin3 against SFTSV and HSV-1.
abstract: Antiviral peptides, as an important source of antiviral drugs, will have significant application value and potential in the field of viral prevention and treatment. Therefore, it is of great significance to discover broad-spectrum, highly efficient, and low-toxicity antiviral peptides. Here, we found that the scorpion venom peptide BmKDfsin3 not only concentration-dependently inhibited the replication of severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus (SFTSV) but also suppressed the replication of herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) in A549 cells. The results of antiviral phase assays showed that BmKDfsin3 mainly inhibited the post-entry stage of the life cycle of these two viruses. Mechanistically, BmKDfsin3 effectively suppressed the activation of p38 induced by SFTSV and HSV-1 infections. Furthermore, using poly(I:C) as a viral mimic, we found that BmKDfsin3 enhanced type I and III interferon signaling pathways by activating the transcription factors p52 and IRF3. Importantly, BmKDfsin3 exhibited good biosafety, including low cytotoxicity, hemolytic activity, and mouse toxicity. Overall, BmKDfsin3 was revealed to be a natural bioactive peptide with good biological safety, potent antiviral activity, and a broad antiviral spectrum. The scorpion venom peptide BmKDfsin3 mediates antiviral activity through a dual mechanism: it limits viral replication by inhibiting the exploitation of host p38 signaling by SFTSV and HSV-1, and it promotes host immune responses by activating transcription factors p52 and IRF3 to enhance type I and III interferon (IFN) signaling. This synergy between "inhibiting virus-dependent pathway" and "activating host immunity" confers potent, broad-spectrum antiviral activity upon BmKDfsin3, resulting in significant dose-dependent inhibition against phylogenetically distinct RNA (SFTSV) and DNA (HSV-1) viruses. Importantly, the peptide exhibits minimal cytotoxicity, hemolytic activity, and in vivo toxicity. This study provides new insights into how a single-peptide molecule achieves efficient, broad-spectrum antiviral activity by concurrently targeting virus-dependent and host immune pathways, highlighting the therapeutic potential of antiviral peptides in broad-spectrum drug design.

title: Decoupling of Cell Volume From the Number of Ribosomal DNA Repeat Copies Through Regulation of RNA Polymerase I Transcription Elongation in a Large-Cell Yeast Mutant.
abstract: Although most studies in the regulation of gene transcription in eukaryotes have focused on protein-coding genes transcribed into mRNA by RNA polymerase II, the regulation of RNA polymerase I (RNA Pol I) transcription is a key step in the cell's adaptation to environmental or physiological changes. This polymerase transcribes rRNA, a fundamental component of ribosomes that controls the translation of mRNAs into proteins-macromolecules that are both highly abundant and energetically costly to synthesize. Using the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae as a model, we have previously shown that adaptation of RNA Pol I synthesis rate (SR) to large changes in cell volume exhibited by some mutants, such as cln3, occurs over the long term through amplification of rDNA gene copies across several hundred cell divisions. However, it remains unclear what happens in the short term in de novo generated mutants that do not display rDNA amplification but exhibit all other phenotypic characteristics of the evolved cln3 mutant. Here, using an in vivo labeling procedure, we show that the RNA Pol I SR is similar in de novo and evolved cln3 mutants and that it seems not to be an alteration in the proportion of active rDNA copies or rRNA processing between both cln3 mutants. Finally, by measuring the ratio of active elongating RNA Pol I molecules to the total loaded onto rDNA genes, we conclude that short-term adaptation occurs through an increase in their transcription efficiency that compensates the decrease in the total number of elongating RNA polymerases.

title: Long Non-Coding RNA H19 Protection Against Myocardial Ischemia/Reperfusion Injury in Diabetic Mice Through Hypoxia-Inducible Factor 1 Alpha Signaling.
abstract: Diabetes can aggravate myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury (MIRI), but the role of long non-coding RNA H19 (lncRNA H19) is still unclear. The purpose of this study was to investigate the effect of lncRNA H19 on MIRI in diabetic mice. C57BL/KsJ db/db diabetes mice and db/+ normal mice (n = 40/group) were divided into sham operation, ischemia/reperfusion (I/R), and I/R+Lv-H19 (lentivirus-mediated H19 overexpression) groups. Echocardiography evaluation of cardiac function and Evans Blue/triphenyltetrazolium chloride staining were used to determine the infarct area; terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase dUTP nick end labeling (TUNEL) and caspase-3 to detect cell apoptosis; western blot to detect autophagy markers (LC3-II/I, p62) and HIF-1α protein expression; and dual luciferase reporter genes to validate the competitive endogenous RNA (ceRNA) mechanism. H19 expression in the hearts of diabetic mice after I/R was significantly lower than that of normal mice (P < 0.05). H19 overexpression significantly improved cardiac function (left ventricular ejection fraction and fractional shortening restored to near-normal levels), reduced infarct size, and lowered serum CK, CK-MB, and LDH levels (P < 0.05). H19 overexpression regulated autophagic flow (LC3-II/I ratio and p62 expression reversal) and inhibited caspase-3 activity (P < 0.05). Mechanistically, H19 acts as a ceRNA for miR-4735-3p, releasing its inhibition of hypoxia-inducible factor 1 alpha (HIF-1α) and activating the HIF-1α signaling pathway. The results of this study provide mechanistic insight into the molecular processes underlying myocardial I/R injury in diabetic mice and identify LNCRNA H19 as a candidate target for further preclinical research.

title: Systems-level phosphoproteomics reveals calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase kinase 2-driven kinase signaling underlying malignant phenotypes in gastric cancer.
abstract: Gastric cancer (GC) is driven by aberrant kinase signaling that promotes uncontrolled proliferation and malignant progression. Calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase kinase 2 (CAMKK2) is overexpressed in GC; however, the global phosphorylation networks downstream of CAMKK2 remain incompletely defined. In this study, we investigated the functional and signaling consequences of CAMKK2 inhibition in GC cells using an integrated phenotypic and quantitative phosphoproteomics approach. Pharmacological inhibition of CAMKK2 using STO-609 in AGS cells significantly suppressed proliferation, clonogenic growth, migration, and invasion and induced defects in nuclear morphology indicative of impaired cell cycle progression. Tandem mass tag-based phosphoproteomic profiling identified over 10,500 phosphopeptides and revealed extensive phosphoproteome remodeling after CAMKK2 inhibition, characterized predominantly by hypophosphorylation of proteins involved in nuclear signaling, RNA processing, and cell cycle regulation. Kinase-substrate enrichment and motif analyses demonstrated coordinated attenuation of cyclin-dependent kinase, mitogen-activated protein kinase, and mitotic kinase-associated signaling pathways, with convergence on E2F-regulated transcriptional programs. Collectively, these findings establish CAMKK2 as a central regulator of kinase signaling networks that sustain proliferative and malignant phenotypes in GC and highlight CAMKK2 inhibition as a potential therapeutic strategy.

title: Natural killer cell-derived extracellular vesicles in cancer: mediators of intercellular communication and tumor immune signaling.
abstract: Natural killer (NK) cells are essential components of innate immunity and play a pivotal role in tumor surveillance through direct cytotoxicity and immune regulation. In recent years, NK-cell-derived extracellular vesicles (NK-EVs) have emerged as a promising cell-free therapeutic modality that preserves key antitumor functions of parental NK cells while overcoming several limitations associated with cell-based immunotherapy. As biologically derived nanovesicles, NK-EVs combine nanoscale delivery properties with a cell-free formulation format and generally low immunogenicity. However, although selected preclinical studies suggest tumor-interacting or target-cell-recognition properties, a broadly applicable intrinsic tumor-targeting capacity-and, in particular, intrinsic blood-brain barrier (BBB) penetration-has not been established for native NK-EVs. This review systematically summarizes the biological characteristics, biogenesis pathways, and molecular cargo of NK-EVs, with particular emphasis on their antitumor mechanisms. Current evidence supports perforin/granzyme-mediated cytotoxicity and Fas/Fas ligand (FasL) signaling as the most established mechanisms of NK-EVs-mediated tumor killing, whereas miRNA-mediated regulation and tumor microenvironment remodeling represent emerging functional pathways requiring further validation. By contrast, tumor necrosis factor-related apoptosis-inducing ligand (TRAIL)-death receptor 4/5 (DR4/DR5) signaling remains putative because direct NK-EVs-specific causal evidence is limited. Functionally investigated miRNAs and tumor-microenvironment effects represent context-dependent or emerging pathways whose generalizability across NK-cell sources and preparation conditions requires further validation. Importantly, recent advances in engineering strategies-including parental-cell priming, cargo loading, antigen-recognition engineering, tissue/barrier-targeting modification, biomimetic nanovesicle construction, and formulation-based stabilization. These approaches can alter cargo composition, recipient-cell recognition, or tissue-specific delivery through distinct mechanisms. Improvements achieved by engineered composite platforms should therefore not be conflated with intrinsic properties of native NK-EVs. Nevertheless, major translational challenges remain, including scalable manufacturing, purification and characterization standardization, mechanism-linked potency testing, biodistribution uncertainty, batch comparability, and product-specific regulatory considerations. Overall, NK-EVs should be viewed not only as potential cell-free therapeutic tools but also as specialized mediators of tumor-immune communication that integrate cytotoxic protein transfer, receptor-mediated signaling, RNA-based regulation, and microenvironmental crosstalk.

title: Interpreting antiviral effects: from experimental measurements to mechanistic viral dynamics.
abstract: Antiviral activity is commonly summarized using endpoint measures such as EC50 or EC90, yet these quantities emerge from a dynamic biological system and depend on viral replication kinetics, host-cell properties, experimental design, and the assay used to quantify infection. Infectious-virus titers, viral RNA, infected-cell fractions, viability measurements, and immune readouts capture different components of the infection process and are therefore not interchangeable measures of "viral load." Mechanistic viral-dynamics models provide a framework for linking such observations to underlying processes, including cell infection, intracellular replication, virus production, cell loss, and host-mediated control. However, the biological information that can be recovered from these models is fundamentally constrained by experimental observability and parameter identifiability. This limitation becomes increasingly important across biological scales: in vitro systems permit dense multimodal measurements and controlled perturbations, whereas animal and human studies provide greater physiological relevance but substantially sparser and more indirect observations. Here, we review how experimental readouts map onto viral-dynamics models, how model structure and parameter inference affect mechanistic interpretation, and how controlled in vitro systems can be used to distinguish competing mechanisms of infection and antiviral action. We further discuss examples in which viral-dynamics modeling has contributed to antiviral pharmacology and regimen selection. Together, these considerations support a view of antiviral effects as context-dependent dynamic phenotypes that require joint interpretation of measurements, models, and experimental design.

title: SARS-CoV-2 ORF6 protein targets IFP35 to inhibit the IFNγ signaling pathway.
abstract: The innate immune system functions as the frontline barrier against invading pathogens, such as severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus-2 (SARS-CoV-2). Nevertheless, the virus has developed various strategies to effectively regulate host immune responses, particularly through the inhibition of interferon signaling. In this study, we identify the SARS-CoV-2 accessory protein ORF6 as a key inhibitor of interferon gamma (IFNγ) signaling through downregulation of the interferon-induced 35-kDa protein (IFP35). IFP35, an interferon-stimulated gene (ISG) critical for interferon -mediated antiviral response, is significantly upregulated during SARS-CoV-2 infection. Silencing IFP35 via RNA interference enhances viral replication, indicating its antiviral role. Furthermore, we demonstrate that ORF6 associates with IFP35 and accelerates its ubiquitin-proteasome degradation, thereby impairing IFP35's ability to activate IFNγ signaling. These data reveal novel mechanisms used by SARS-CoV-2 to circumvent host immunity, specifically by impairing IFNγ signaling.

title: Glial Scar-Targeted Modification of Hepatocyte Growth Factor-Derived Peptide for Spinal Cord Injury Therapeutic Repair.
abstract: Spinal cord injury (SCI) causes irreversible neural damage and functional impairment. H-RN is a short peptide originating from the kringle 1 domain of hepatocyte growth factor. Despite its efficacy in inhibiting inflammatory responses, the precise neuroprotective mechanisms of the peptide H-RN in SCI remain unclear. The short peptide CAQK can target the lesion epicenter of SCI. To explore the role of the peptide H-RN in SCI and address the numerous challenges faced by conventional drug therapies, this study developed a synthetic peptide, CAQK-H-RN. Our results revealed that CAQK-H-RN could cross the blood-spinal cord barrier, precisely target the SCI region, and increase drug accumulation at the injury site, thereby reducing glial scar formation, decreasing motor neuron death, and enhancing functional recovery after SCI. RNA sequencing was performed to explore the molecular mechanisms of CAQK-H-RN in SCI, which revealed that CAQK-H-RN inhibited pyroptosis and ameliorated lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP)-induced autophagic flux disorders in neurons after SCI. Additionally, CAQK-H-RN alleviated LMP by suppressing acid sphingomyelinase activity through the p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase/Ets-like protein-1 (Elk-1)/early growth response protein 1 (Egr-1) signaling cascade and subsequently enhanced autophagy, thereby mitigating neuronal death. This intravenous therapeutic system centered on the synthetic peptide CAQK-H-RN contributes to the functional restoration of SCI, which may be clinically applicable to spinal cord repair.

title: Genome-wide identification of the BES1 gene family and functional study of VcBES1.3 under salt stress in blueberry (Vaccinium corymbosum).
abstract: BES1 (BRI1-EMS-SUPPRESSOR 1) transcription factors mediate brassinosteroid signaling and regulate plant growth, development, and stress responses. The BES1 family has not been characterized in blueberry (Vaccinium corymbosum L.). We identified 16 VcBES1 family members and classified them into four groups based on phylogenetic analysis. Promoters of the BES1 genes mainly contain cis-elements associated with abiotic stress and phytohormone signaling. Tissue-specific expression analysis showed that the VcBES1 family is expressed predominantly in roots and stems. All members except VcBES1.8 and VcBES1.9 responded positively to salt stress. Among them, VcBES1.3 displayed the strongest salt induction. The protein accumulated in the nucleus. Overexpression and RNA interference (RNAi) experiments established that VcBES1.3 enhances salt tolerance. This study characterizes the VcBES1 family, defines its tissue-specific and stress-responsive expression patterns, and demonstrate that VcBES1.3 as a positive regulator of salt tolerance in blueberry.

title: Maize endonuclease NOB1 couples ribosome biogenesis with translational regulation during kernel development.
abstract: NOB1-mediated cleavage of 20S pre-rRNA represents a critical quality-control step during cytoplasmic maturation of the eukaryotic 40S ribosomal subunit, yet its developmental significance in crops remains largely unexplored. Here, we identified two highly conserved maize NOB1 paralogs, ZmNOB1a and ZmNOB1b, both exhibiting RNA-binding and endonuclease activities and associating with pre-40S ribosomal particles. Genetic analyses demonstrated that the two paralogs function redundantly, but with unequal contributions, to support gametophyte viability and kernel development. Simultaneous disruption of ZmNOB1 activity resulted in severely impaired male gametophyte transmission, markeldly reduced female gamete viability, and profound defects in embryo and endosperm development. Molecular analyses further revealed widespread disruption of pre-rRNA maturation, including defective D-site cleavage, accompanied by impaired ribosome assembly and reduced translational capacity. Consistent with these molecular defects, mutant kernels exhibited decreased starch and storage protein accumulation, together with elevated levels of free ribosomal subunits and reduced 80S monosomes and polysomes. Moreover, ZmNOB1 exhibited co-sedimentation and directly interacted with the translation initiation factor eIF4A, implying a potential functional coordination between late ribosome maturation and translation initiation. Collectively, our findings establish ZmNOB1-mediated pre-rRNA processing as a key determinant of translational competence, reproductive fitness, and seed filling in maize.

title: A novel venom protein from the parasitoid Pteromalus puparum suppresses host melanization by targeting multiple components of the prophenoloxidase cascade.
abstract: Parasitoid venom proteins are known to manipulate host immunity and metabolism. In the present study, a novel venom protein from the parasitoid Pteromalus puparum (Linnaeus) (Hymenoptera: Pteromalidae) (PpVPG) was identified and functional analyses of PpVPG were conducted. PpVPG is abundantly expressed in the venom apparatus, has a low molecular weight, and is a lineage‑specific venom protein with no functional annotation available. Functional analysis via RNA interference revealed that PpVPG is essential for parasitism, as its silencing severely impaired successful parasitism of Pieris rapae (Linnaeus) (Lepidoptera: Pieridae), a major Brassicaceae pest worldwide. Biochemical characterization showed that recombinant PpVPG inhibited PO activation in host hemolymph in a dose-dependent manner but had no effect on pre-activated PO, indicating that it acts upstream of PO activation. Both the N-terminal and C-terminal fragments retained partial inhibitory activity. Target identification by affinity purification coupled with mass spectrometry identified three host proteins as direct interaction partners of PpVPG: two prophenoloxidases (PrPPO1, PrPPO2) and a prophenoloxidase-activating factor (PrPAF2). Surface plasmon resonance confirmed high-affinity binding of PpVPG to these three proteins, as well as to a prophenoloxidase-activating protease (PrPAP1). This multi-target binding strategy, engaging both the zymogen substrates and their activation machinery within a single immune cascade, represents an effective molecular strategy for a small, non-enzymatic venom protein. These findings establish PpVPG as a venom effector that suppresses host melanization through multi-target binding.

title: Targeting circular RNAs to overcome therapeutic resistance in liver cancer: from mechanisms to clinical prospects.
abstract: Primary liver cancer, including hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (iCCA), remains a leading cause of cancer-related death worldwide. Therapeutic resistance substantially limits the efficacy of chemotherapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and radiotherapy. For example, only approximately 30% of patients with HCC derive clinical benefit from sorafenib, and acquired resistance commonly develops within six months, underscoring the urgent need to clarify the molecular basis of treatment failure. Circular RNAs (circRNAs) are covalently closed RNA molecules with high structural stability and tissue-specific expression. In liver cancer, circRNAs regulate therapeutic resistance through multiple mechanisms that converge on ferroptosis suppression, apoptosis evasion, DNA damage repair, oncogenic signaling, immune escape, and cancer stemness. Beyond the canonical competing endogenous RNA model, this review highlights emerging regulatory mechanisms involving RNA-binding protein interactions, circRNA-encoded functional micropeptides, and circRNA-mediated phase separation. Exosomal circRNAs also facilitate the intercellular transmission of resistant phenotypes and remodel the tumor immune microenvironment. We systematically summarize circRNA-mediated resistance across different therapeutic modalities and critically evaluate the available evidence according to experimental models, in vivo validation, and patient validation. Although circRNAs show potential as biomarkers for predicting therapeutic response and as targets for overcoming resistance, most candidates remain at the preclinical stage. Their clinical translation is constrained by the lack of standardized detection methods, insufficient multicenter validation, and inefficient and inadequately targeted in vivo delivery systems. Because most direct mechanistic evidence is derived from HCC, selected iCCA-related findings are incorporated where available.

title: ALK-positive large B-cell lymphoma with plasmacytoid predominance and a novel CEP128::ALK fusion.
abstract: ALK-positive large B-cell lymphoma (ALK+ LBCL) is a diffuse, monomorphic neoplasm of large B-cells with a plasmablastic immunophenotype and ALK expression due to ALK rearrangements. We report a diagnostically deceptive case in a 51-year-old woman with a small localized bronchial lesion. Histology showed sheets of mature to mildly enlarged plasmacytoid cells with scattered multinucleated forms and rare large atypical cells. The tumor expressed CD38, CD138, MUM1, and CD79a, but lacked CD20, CD30, and EBER. No bone marrow involvement, monoclonal protein, bone lesions, or systemic disease was detected, initially suggesting extramedullary plasmacytoma. However, ALK immunohistochemistry revealed paranuclear dot-like cytoplasmic staining, and FISH confirmed ALK rearrangement. DNA- and RNA-based sequencing identified a novel in-frame CEP128::ALK fusion retaining the ALK tyrosine kinase domain. This case broadens the molecular spectrum of ALK-positive LBCL and highlights ALK testing in localized CD20-negative plasmacytoid lesions.

title: A small modification makes a big difference: rRNA modifications in hematopoiesis and leukemia.
abstract: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) sustain lifelong blood production through a fine balance between self-renewal and differentiation that demands a tight regulation of protein synthesis. HSCs are highly sensitive to translational perturbation, as exemplified by human ribosomopathies-a group of congenital bone marrow failure syndromes caused by mutations in ribosomal components and biogenesis factors. While the contribution of ribosome numbers to hematologic disease is established, ribosome composition is emerging as an equally important axis of regulation. A central source of this compositional diversity is ribosomal RNA (rRNA) nucleotide modifications-human rRNAs carry over 200 chemical modifications, primarily 2'-O-methylation and pseudouridylation, which were long regarded as static structural features but are now recognized as dynamically regulated during cellular differentiation. Perturbation of these modification patterns has profound consequences. In dyskeratosis congenita, germline mutations to rRNA modification-related proteins disrupt rRNA modifications landscape, and cause bone marrow failure through selective translational defects without globally compromising ribosomes numbers. Conversely, in acute myeloid leukemia, leukemic stem cells actively maintain high rRNA modification levels at specific sites to sustain self-renewal, metabolic fitness, and chemoresistance, effectively driving a stem-like translational state. In this review, we integrate findings from normal hematopoietic differentiation, congenital bone marrow failure syndromes, and leukemia to describe how rRNA modifications link translation to cell fate in the hematopoietic system. We discuss the dynamics of rRNA modifications as determinants of cellular identity and highlight emerging therapeutic opportunities, as well as the significant gaps that remain in this expanding field.

title: Empirical substitution models of evolution for protein phylogenetics of the Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus.
abstract: Probabilistic methods for phylogenetic inference rely on substitution models of molecular evolution. However, at the protein level, the availability of empirical substitution models remains limited, particularly for viruses. Here, we present empirical substitution models of protein evolution for several Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) proteins, including the nucleoprotein, glycoprotein precursor, and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase. For each protein, we estimated the exchangeability matrix and amino acid frequencies at equilibrium from hundreds of sequences using maximum likelihood, and we evaluated the models using independent data. The inferred CCHFV models revealed distinct evolutionary patterns among viral proteins, including patterns in polar and glycosylation-associated regions, while generally preserving common physicochemical features such as amino acid charge, polarity, and hydrophobic packing shaped by selective pressures. Remarkably, the CCHFV protein substitution models consistently outperformed all currently available empirical substitution models, including those inferred from other viral proteins, in terms of phylogenetic likelihood with independent CCHFV protein sequences. These findings support the use of these substitution models to improve the accuracy of phylogenetic reconstructions of CCHFV proteins, thereby enabling more reliable inference of evolutionary trajectories that may be useful for therapeutic design.

title: TDP-43 dysfunction destabilizes glial homeostatic identity in ALS/FTD.
abstract: TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) pathology is a defining feature of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD). Although TDP-43 dysfunction has traditionally been studied through a neuron-centric framework, increasing evidence demonstrates that astrocytes, microglia, and oligodendrocytes are also directly affected and actively contribute to disease progression. In this review, we examine how TDP-43 dysfunction disrupts lineage-specific glial homeostatic programs and promotes distinct pathological state transitions across major glial populations. In astrocytes, TDP-43 dysfunction impairs neurotransmitter regulation, metabolic and neuronal support, RNA homeostasis, and secretory signaling while promoting inflammatory and antiviral-like states. In microglia, altered TDP-43 disrupts inflammatory regulation, phagocytosis, lysosomal function, lipid metabolism, and stage-dependent protective responses. In oligodendrocytes, TDP-43 dysfunction compromises RNA processing, lineage maintenance, lipid metabolism, myelin integrity, and long-term axonal support. Together, these findings suggest that glial TDP-43 dysfunction cannot be reduced to a single generalized form of reactivity but instead reflects the breakdown of distinct cell type-specific identities required to maintain central nervous system homeostasis. A cross-glial framework integrating cell-autonomous dysfunction, non-cell-autonomous signaling, disease stage, and genetic context may therefore provide a more complete understanding of TDP-43 proteinopathy and its contribution to neurodegeneration across the ALS-FTD spectrum.

title: STRADA deficiency impairs cortical interneuron development in humans and mice.
abstract: Polyhydramnios, Megalencephaly, and Symptomatic Epilepsy syndrome (PMSE/STRADA-related disease) is a rare neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by megalencephaly, early-onset drug-resistant epilepsy, neurocognitive impairment, and high early mortality, often due to status epilepticus. PMSE is caused by a multiexon deletion in the STRADA/LYK5 gene, encoding STRADA protein, which regulates the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway. GABAergic inhibitory interneurons (INs) critically modulate excitatory:inhibitory balance in cortical networks, and IN deficits contribute to epileptogenesis in several epileptic encephalopathies. However, no studies to date have investigated INs in PMSE. We demonstrate that Strada/STRADA loss causes a reduction of multiple IN subtypes in the cerebral cortex and a corresponding increase in the striatum, representative of the remnant ganglionic eminence progenitor origin, in both Strada-/- mice and in a case of human PMSE brain tissue, suggestive of an IN migration defect. RNA sequencing comparing wildtype control to Strada-/- mouse cortex and striatum corroborates these findings, revealing increased IN-related gene expression (e.g., Dlx2) in the striatum. mTOR-associated genes (Lamp5, Cryab) are differentially expressed in the developing cortex, and cytoskeletal-associated genes (e.g., Tppp3, Kank4, Map1a) are differentially expressed in the developing cortex and mature striatum of Strada-/- mice. Functional validation confirms enlarged INs in Strada/STRADA-deficient brain, associated with mTOR hyperactivation. Together, these results suggest that STRADA/Strada loss may contribute to failed IN migration, the first such report in a developmental mTORassociated megalencephaly syndrome, highlighting INs as a therapeutic target for seizure prevention in PMSE.

title: Non-canonical nucleic acid structures in viruses: Regulatory modules and emerging antiviral targets.
abstract: Beyond their primary sequence, viral genomes contain structural information encoded in the ability of DNA and RNA to fold into alternative conformations. These dynamic non-canonical nucleic acid structures include G-quadruplexes (G4s), i-Motifs (iMs), R-loops, G4-associated R-loops and left-handed Z-conformations. Among them, G4s have been most extensively investigated in viruses and have been reported to modulate transcription, replication, translation, latency and immune evasion. However, the functional interpretation of these structures remains highly context-dependent: similar topologies can either promote or restrict infection depending on genomic location, folding dynamics, protein interactors and the stage of the viral life cycle. Here, we discuss recent advances in viral non-canonical nucleic acid structures, emphasizing the level of evidence supporting their formation and function. We also assess emerging antiviral strategies based on structure-targeting ligands, highlighting both their translational potential and the unresolved challenges of selectivity, target engagement and pharmacological validation in infected cells.

title: Esculetin alleviates mouse transplant rejection by modulating CD4+ T cell functional responses and glycolytic metabolism via the PI3K-AKT-mTOR axis.
abstract: Immune rejection is a major cause of graft dysfunction following organ transplantation, and CD4+ T cells play a critical role in this process. Esculetin is a natural coumarin compound derived from the Chinese herbal medicine Fraxinus. Although its anti-tumor and anti-inflammatory effects have been extensively investigated, its potential role in transplant immunology remains unexplored. The effect of esculetin on transplant rejection and CD4+ T cells was evaluated by survival curve analysis, H&E staining, immunohistochemical staining, flow cytometry, and RNA sequencing. The effects of esculetin on the phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)-protein kinase B (AKT)-mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway, cell cycle, apoptosis, and glycolytic metabolism in CD4+ T cells were also examined. The functional rescue experiments were performed by combining esculetin with the PI3K activator 740Y-P and inhibitor LY294002. Esculetin prolonged graft survival and attenuated graft injury. In addition, esculetin treatment suppressed CD4+ T cell functional responses. RNA sequencing of cultured CD4+ T cells revealed that genes downregulated by esculetin were enriched in the PI3K-AKT and cell cycle pathways. Mechanistically, esculetin inhibited PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling, glycolysis, and cell cycle progression, while promoting apoptosis in CD4+ T cells. Furthermore, rescue experiments using PI3K modulators confirmed that esculetin acts through this pathway to suppress proliferation, induce apoptosis, and prolong graft survival. The present study is the first to demonstrate that esculetin attenuates immune rejection in mouse skin and heart transplantation models by modulating the PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling pathway in CD4+ T cells, thereby exerting inhibitory effects on proliferation, induction of apoptosis, and suppression of glycolytic metabolism.

title: Novel amidino-substituted phenylene-bis(benzazoles): Design, synthesis, biological evaluation and DNA binding properties.
abstract: A series of symmetrical amidino-substituted phenylene-bis(benzazoles) incorporating benzoxazole, benzothiazole and benzimidazole scaffolds was designed to explore the influence of the heteroaromatic core, substitution pattern and amidine type on antiproliferative and antitrypanosomal activity. Distinct structure-activity relationships were observed for the two biological activity profiles. Antiproliferative activity strongly depended on both the heteroaromatic scaffold and the nature of the amidine moiety. Among the investigated series, bis(benzoxazoles) showed the highest potency, with C-6 imidazolinyl derivatives 7da and 7 db displaying submicromolar inhibitory activity across a panel of human cancer cell lines (EC50 = 0.06-2.5 μM). Evaluation in PBMCs indicated cancer cell selectivity, while cell cycle analysis of the most active derivatives revealed G2/M phase accumulation. In contrast, antitrypanosomal activity against bloodstream-form Trypanosoma brucei followed a different SAR profile, with several derivatives showing pronounced potency and favourable selectivity indices. In particular, the benzoxazole derivative 7 ab bearing an unsubstituted amidine exhibited excellent potency and selectivity (EC50 = 0.044 μM, SI = 920), while the benzothiazole derivative 3aa also demonstrated strong activity (EC50 = 0.09 μM, SI = 325). In the benzimidazole series, the imidazolinyl derivative 9ba showed a highly favourable profile (EC50 = 0.05 μM, SI = 675). Biophysical studies revealed that 9ba exhibits high affinity toward AT-rich nucleic acid structures, including triplex DNA and DNA:RNA hybrids. Integration of biological and biophysical data indicates that nucleic acid recognition may contribute to the biological activity of this series. Overall, the distinct SAR profiles identified 7 ab as the most promising antitrypanosomal lead for further optimization towards the development of potent and selective antitrypanosomal agents.

title: Paperclip RNAs bypass clathrin mediated endocytosis in insect and fungal cells.
abstract: Insects and fungi are among the most destructive pests and pathogens affecting agriculture and public health. Although chemical pesticides have long been the primary means of control, their broad‑spectrum activity and widespread use have accelerated resistance in many systems. RNA interference (RNAi) has therefore emerged as a promising species‑specific alternative. RNAi is initiated by double‑stranded RNA (dsRNA), which triggers sequence‑directed degradation of target transcripts. However, RNAi efficiency varies markedly across species, influenced by nuclease activity, dsRNA length, and the cellular uptake route. We previously showed that long dsRNA uptake in Aedes aegypti depends on clathrin‑mediated endocytosis (CME), whereas paperclip RNA (pcRNA), a compact dsRNA structure developed in our laboratory, bypasses CME and enters cells through a distinct pathway. Here, we compared the uptake and RNAi performance of two dsRNA formats, long dsRNA (210-230 bp) and pcRNA (21-23 bp), in three representative species: Aedes aegypti (mosquito), Spodoptera frugiperda (moth), and Sclerotinia sclerotiorum (fungus). To assess cellular uptake of these dsRNAs, we used two CME inhibitors, chlorpromazine (CPZ) and bafilomycin A1 (BafA1), along with fluorescein‑labeled dsRNAs. CME inhibition prevented long dsRNA from entering the cytoplasm and abolished its ability to induce RNAi. In contrast, pcRNAs were readily internalized and produced significant gene knockdowns under both inhibitor treatments. Microscopy further revealed that all three cell types, pretreated with either CPZ or BafA1, prevented long dsRNA from entering the cytoplasm. pcRNA, consistently reached the cytoplasm and showed superior uptake across all species. Together, these findings demonstrate that pcRNA uses an uptake mechanism distinct from long dsRNA, enabling it to circumvent CME-dependent barriers. This unique internalization route likely reflects its compact size and structural configuration and highlights pcRNA as a promising platform for improving RNAi-based pest and pathogen control.

title: The role of cardiomyocytic FOXP3 and extracellular vesicle-mediated delivery of FOXP3 into cardiomyocytes for treating pathological cardiac hypertrophy.
abstract: While forkhead helix transcription factor P3 (FOXP3) is a key regulator in T cells, we previously reported its anti-hypertrophic role in cardiomyocytes. In the present study, by overexpressing FOXP3 and using RNA-seq, we found that FOXP3 suppresses pathological cardiac hypertrophy by upregulating ferritin heavy chain 1, thereby inhibiting ferroptosis. However, data from the single-RNA sequence database showed that the in vivo cardiomyocytes exhibit minimal Foxp3 mRNA, despite the presence of FOXP3 protein. Here, we identified cardiac microenvironment-derived extracellular vesicles (cEVs) carrying FOXP3 protein as the source of cardiomyocytic FOXP3. Leveraging this intercellular delivery mechanism, we demonstrate that administering FOXP3+ cEVs from healthy hearts mitigates isoproterenol (ISO)-induced ferroptosis and hypertrophy. Due to the impracticality of large-scale production of cEVs, we identified the Jurkat cell as an alternative source of FOXP3+ EVs. The Jurkat cell-derived EVs (jEVs) increased the content of cardiomyocytic FOXP3, thereby reversing hypertrophic responses. Moreover, we engineered Jurkat cells to increase FOXP3 content in the jEVs, thereby obtaining FOXP3-enriched jEVs that exhibited superior attenuation of hypertrophy and suppression of ferroptosis compared to native EVs. These findings suggest that increasing the content of FOXP3 protein in cardiomyocytes through engineered FOXP3-enriched extracellular vesicles offers a novel strategy for treating cardiac hypertrophy.

title: M6A-modified lncRNA RMRP facilitates mitophagy and promotes ox-LDL-induced endothelial cell injury by interacting with PTBP1 and activating the PI3K/AKT pathway.
abstract: Endothelial cell dysfunction has been identified as a major risk factor for atherosclerosis. The long non-coding RNA (LncRNA) RNA component of mitochondrial RNA processing endoribonuclease (RMRP) has been detected in mitochondria and is closely associated with inflammation and autophagy. However, the role of the lncRNA RMRP in endothelial cell injury and its potential molecular mechanisms remain unclear. Mouse aortic endothelial cells (MAECs) were treated with oxidised low-density lipoprotein (ox-LDL). Changes in cell viability, proinflammatory cytokine levels, mitophagy, and mitochondrial membrane potential in MAECs were assessed to investigate the effects of lncRNA RMRP and protein kinase B (AKT3) on endothelial injury. Knockdown and overexpression experiments were performed to determine the effects of lncRNA RMRP, polypyrimidine tract-binding protein 1 (PTBP1), and AKT3 on MAECs stimulated with ox-LDL. Ox-LDL markedly reduced cell viability, increased proinflammatory factor levels, induced mitophagy, and reduced mitochondrial membrane potential in MAECs. Knockdown of lncRNA RMRP attenuated ox-LDL-induced inflammatory responses and mitophagy in MAECs. Knockdown of Methyltransferase-like 14 (METTL14) suppressed the expression of lncRNA RMRP through m6A modification in ox-LDL-treated MAECs. LncRNA RMRP enhanced AKT3 mRNA stability by interacting with PTBP1. LncRNA RMRP promoted ox-LDL-induced mitophagy by targeting AKT3 and stimulating the Phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/AKT pathway in MAECs. METTL14 regulates the expression of lncRNA RMRP through m6A modification. Overexpressed lncRNA RMRP targets AKT3 by recruiting PTBP1, thus activating the PI3K/AKT pathway to mediate mitophagy and promote the progression of atherosclerosis.
